title: Homeowner directly identifies themselves during registration
description: During account registration, the homeowner provides directly identifying account data such as name, email address, phone number, or username to the Home Hub. The act of sharing this data makes the individual identifiable to the system.
assumptions: Assumes registration requires account identifiers rather than being fully anonymous or pseudonymous.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Enrollment data can link the homeowner to specific devices
description: By enrolling cameras and sensors on the Home Hub, the homeowner shares device identifiers, device inventory, and configuration context that can be linked to the same account, allowing correlation between the person and a set of household devices.
assumptions: Assumes device serial numbers, MAC addresses, model identifiers, or similar enrollment metadata are associated with the registering account.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate; threat applicability is strong but exact node id may differ in the full LINDDUN Pro tree.

title: Data in transit may reveal the homeowner's identity and household context
description: Registration and device-enrollment traffic may contain account identifiers and device metadata in transit. If exposed on the network, this traffic could identify the homeowner or household.
assumptions: Assumes the flow traverses a network where traffic contents or metadata could be observed, especially if transport protections are weak or absent.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is approximate; this is a standard in-transit identifiability threat.

title: Network-visible metadata can link repeated registration or enrollment actions
description: Even if payload contents are protected, traffic metadata such as timing, endpoint addresses, protocol use, and repeated enrollment events may allow an observer to link multiple actions to the same household or account setup session.
assumptions: Assumes an observer can access network metadata for this flow.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate; based on standard linkability-via-metadata reasoning.

title: Home Hub learns detailed household device composition during enrollment
description: On receipt of registration and enrollment data, the Home Hub can infer the presence, number, type, and placement context of cameras and sensors in the home. This reveals private facts about the household's security setup and living environment.
assumptions: Assumes the hub stores or processes device type and configuration details beyond what is strictly necessary for transient setup.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because detailed disclosure nodes were not provided in the retrieved context.

title: Registration and enrollment may occur without sufficient homeowner awareness
description: If the Home Hub does not clearly explain what account and device data are collected, how long they are stored, and for what purposes they are used, the homeowner may be unaware of the privacy implications of registration and device enrollment.
assumptions: Assumes the hub UX may not provide sufficiently clear notice during setup.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; threat depends on actual notice and transparency design.

title: Home Hub may collect more registration or device data than necessary
description: The Home Hub may request or retain excessive personal or device metadata during account creation and device enrollment, such as unnecessary profile fields or detailed device attributes not required for core setup, reducing compliance with data minimization and purpose-limitation expectations.
assumptions: Assumes the implementation collects optional or excessive fields beyond what is strictly needed to register the account and pair devices.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate; framed as a non-compliance risk grounded in minimization/purpose limitation.

title: Guest may be unaware they are sharing personal data when entering the temporary access code
description: When the guest enters the temporary access code at the Home Hub, they may not realize the code entry can be treated as personal data about their visit or presence, especially if the hub logs the event together with time and door-unlock outcome.
assumptions: Assumes the temporary access code is associated with a specific guest, invitation, or visit window, and that the Home Hub or connected system records code-entry events.
uncertainty_note: The applicability depends on whether the code or resulting event is linkable to an identifiable guest and whether the system provides adequate notice.

title: Home Hub can link temporary code entry to a specific guest or visit
description: If the Home Hub stores the temporary access code, invitation identifier, or associated metadata such as timestamp and unlock result, it can link this interaction to a particular guest or household visit pattern.
assumptions: Assumes the hub or backend maintains per-code records or logs that distinguish one guest access code from another.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate; exact LINDDUN Pro subnode may vary depending on whether linkage is via code value, account mapping, or event metadata.

title: Home Hub can identify the guest from the temporary access code
description: A temporary access code that is unique per guest, booking, or invitation can allow the Home Hub to identify or single out the guest behind the interaction, especially when combined with household records or backend invitation data.
assumptions: Assumes codes are unique or otherwise mappable to a guest, reservation, or invitation record.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate; identification may be direct or indirect depending on system design.

title: Code-entry logs may disclose the guest's presence or visit timing
description: By receiving and potentially storing the temporary access code and the time of entry, the Home Hub can learn and later expose sensitive information about when a guest arrived, attempted entry, or was present at the home.
assumptions: Assumes the hub logs entry attempts or unlock events and that such logs are accessible to household members, administrators, or integrated services.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate; the concrete disclosure path depends on logging, retention, and access controls.

title: Guest may have no meaningful choice or consent regarding processing of code-entry data
description: The Home Hub may process and retain the guest's temporary access code and related access-event metadata without offering the guest a practical opportunity to consent, refuse, or understand secondary uses such as logging or analytics.
assumptions: Assumes the guest is not presented with privacy information or controls at the point of code entry.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on the deployment context and whether another channel provided notice and consent.

title: Excessive retention or over-collection of sensor events in the local log
description: The Local Event Log may store more motion/door/sensor event data than is necessary, or retain it longer than needed. Because event histories can reveal occupancy patterns, routines, and behavior inside the home, unnecessary storage constitutes avoidable data disclosure at the destination.
assumptions: The logged events relate to identifiable household members or visitors, directly or by inference from time-stamped in-home activity.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort based on common LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality structure; the retrieved context supports Dd and minimality but does not explicitly list the exact node id.

title: Linkability of household behavior across logged events
description: By accumulating time-stamped motion, door, and sensor events, the Local Event Log can enable linking separate events into patterns attributable to the same household, room, device, or person. This makes it possible to correlate activities over time and infer routines.
assumptions: Events contain stable identifiers, timestamps, device/location labels, or other attributes that permit correlation.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is approximate; applicability of linkability is strong, but the precise node numbering is not confirmed by the provided context.

title: Identifiability through detailed in-home event records
description: Detailed sensor-event logs may allow identification of specific residents or visitors, either directly through identifiers or indirectly through distinctive activity patterns, room usage, and timing. The destination datastore creates this risk by storing and organizing the data.
assumptions: The event log includes timestamps and contextual metadata sufficient to single out individuals or small groups.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is approximate; identifiability is inferred from the nature of smart-home event logs rather than explicitly stated in the prompt.

title: Detectability of presence and absence from event logging
description: The existence and timing of logged motion and door events can make residents' presence, absence, sleep cycles, or arrivals/departures detectable. Even if identities are not explicit, the stored event traces expose whether meaningful activities occurred.
assumptions: An observer with access to the datastore or its outputs can inspect event timing or counts.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is approximate; detectability clearly applies to occupancy/activity inference, but the precise node numbering is not confirmed by the retrieved context.

title: Logging may exceed users' expectations or awareness
description: Residents or visitors may be unaware that fine-grained motion, door, and sensor events are being persistently logged locally, or may not understand the extent of inference possible from those logs. This creates an unawareness threat at the destination where the data is stored.
assumptions: Notice, transparency, or local UI indicators about event logging are limited or absent.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is approximate; unawareness depends on the surrounding product UX and notices, which are not described.

title: Local event logging may occur without valid consent or appropriate choice
description: If the Home Hub writes household activity events to the Local Event Log without obtaining valid consent where required, or without offering meaningful configuration/opt-out choices, the storage creates a non-compliance risk. This is especially relevant for visitors or secondary users whose activities are captured indirectly.
assumptions: Applicable law or policy requires consent, notice, or configurable controls for this category of in-home behavioral data.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on jurisdiction, role of the operator, and legal basis; exact tree node id is approximate.

title: Uploading identifiable video clips discloses residents and visitors to a third party
description: The Home Hub sends recorded camera clips to cloud storage. Video footage can directly reveal faces, bodies, behavior, presence at home, routines, and activities of residents, visitors, delivery personnel, or neighbors. The act of transferring these clips from the home environment to a cloud provider expands disclosure beyond the local context.
assumptions: Recorded clips contain personal data such as recognizable people, voices, timestamps, or contextual household details.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the specific disclosure subtree for this flow.

title: Clip content and transfer metadata may enable identification in transit
description: During upload, the clip payload and associated metadata such as account identifiers, device identifiers, IP address, timestamps, camera names, or location-related labels may identify the household or specific individuals if exposed or insufficiently protected in transit.
assumptions: The upload includes metadata alongside the video clips, and transport protections may be imperfect or metadata may remain visible to intermediaries.
uncertainty_note: Specific identification subtree citation is approximate; applicability depends on what metadata is transmitted and how transport is protected.

title: Repeated uploads can be linked to the same household or device
description: Even if clip contents are not inspected, recurring uploads with stable device, account, network, or timing metadata can allow an observer or intermediary to link multiple uploads to the same home, camera, or user account, building a profile of occupancy and behavior patterns.
assumptions: Uploads use persistent identifiers or otherwise stable metadata such as account tokens, device IDs, IP addresses, or regular timing patterns.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; the linkage risk is genuine but depends on observability of stable metadata.

title: Cloud storage may expose clips to unauthorized internal or external parties
description: Once received by Cloud Video Storage, stored clips may be accessible to cloud administrators, support staff, subprocessors, or attackers if access controls, segregation, or encryption are inadequate. This results in disclosure of highly sensitive in-home footage.
assumptions: Cloud storage personnel or connected services may have some logical access path to stored clips or related metadata.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure subtree citation is based on best judgement rather than retrieved context.

title: Cloud-side secondary use of uploaded clips may exceed user expectations
description: The destination may analyze or reuse uploaded clips and metadata for purposes beyond simple storage, such as service improvement, model training, analytics, law-enforcement response workflows, or cross-service profiling, without users fully understanding or expecting these uses.
assumptions: The cloud provider has technical and contractual ability to process stored clips for additional purposes.
uncertainty_note: Exact unawareness subtree id is approximate; threat depends on provider practices and transparency.

title: Stored camera clips may be retained longer than necessary
description: Cloud Video Storage may keep uploaded clips beyond the period necessary for the stated purpose, contrary to storage limitation obligations. Extended retention increases privacy risk because historical in-home footage remains available for later access, analysis, or disclosure.
assumptions: Retention periods are not strictly minimized, enforced, or communicated, or backups/logs preserve clips beyond expected deletion times.

title: Insufficient evidence of upload, access, and deletion actions can undermine accountability
description: If the cloud storage service does not maintain reliable records of clip receipt, access, sharing, and deletion, the provider or other actors may later deny having received, accessed, or retained specific footage. This impairs users' ability to contest misuse or prove compliance with requests such as deletion.
assumptions: Audit logging, provenance, and deletion evidence may be incomplete or unavailable to users/controllers.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation-related privacy applicability is plausible here, but the exact subtree id is approximate.

title: Home Hub may disclose more motion-alert data than necessary to the backend
description: When forwarding a real-time motion alert, the Home Hub may include excessive personal data beyond what is strictly needed for alert handling, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, household identifiers, sensor state history, or contextual metadata. This creates an avoidable explicit disclosure from the source to the backend.
assumptions: The motion alert concerns activity in a home and is therefore personal data or strongly privacy-relevant. The backend can perform its function with a minimized alert payload.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected as best-fit minimality/excessive disclosure node; exact node numbering may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Real-time motion-alert traffic can identify the household or user by metadata in transit
description: Even if payload contents are protected, flow metadata such as source/destination endpoints, persistent device/backend identifiers, routing information, and timing of repeated alerts can enable identification of a specific household, device, or occupant pattern.
assumptions: Network or intermediary observers can access some communication metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id is approximate; identification via communication metadata is the intended concern.

title: Repeated motion-alert transmissions can be linked into occupancy patterns
description: A sequence of real-time motion alerts over this flow can be correlated by timing, device identifiers, or stable communication characteristics, allowing an observer or recipient to link multiple events to the same home and infer routines such as presence, sleep, or travel patterns.
assumptions: Alerts are associated with stable identifiers or otherwise correlatable metadata over time.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; linkage of multiple events over time is the intended threat.

title: Backend can detect sensitive household activities from motion alerts
description: On receipt of real-time motion alerts, the backend can infer occupancy, daily routines, sleeping patterns, absences, or unusual activity in the home. These inferences may exceed what users expect from simple alert delivery and constitute detectability of sensitive states or events.
assumptions: The backend processes or has access to alert timing/history rather than merely relaying a single opaque message.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; threat is detectability/inference of sensitive events from received alerts.

title: Backend storage or further use of motion alerts may cause avoidable disclosure
description: After receiving the alert, the backend may store, analyze, or share motion-event data more broadly than necessary for immediate notification, causing additional disclosure of in-home activity data to internal services, operators, or third parties.
assumptions: The backend retains or rediscloses alert data beyond transient delivery.
uncertainty_note: Exact node numbering is approximate; concern is onward/secondary disclosure at the destination.

title: Users may be unaware that backend processing of motion alerts reveals occupancy patterns
description: If the system does not clearly communicate that motion alerts sent to the backend can be retained, analyzed, or used to derive household behavior patterns, users may lack awareness of the privacy impact of this data flow.
assumptions: Transparency about backend-side processing is incomplete or not salient to users.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; threat is insufficient user awareness regarding backend processing.

title: Backend processing of motion alerts may exceed or conflict with user consent
description: If users consent only to immediate alert delivery, but the backend also retains alerts, performs analytics, or uses them for secondary purposes, the destination processing may not be compliant with the user's consent or stated privacy choices.
assumptions: Consent or privacy preferences are scoped narrowly and may not cover all backend uses of motion-alert data.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; threat depends on actual consent scope and backend practices.

title: Notification reveals more personal data than necessary
description: The backend may include excessive detail in the motion-detected push notification (for example exact timestamps, room/camera identifiers, thumbnails, or repeated event context) when a less detailed alert would suffice. This constitutes avoidable disclosure of personal data to the homeowner device/user beyond data minimisation needs for the alerting purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the notification payload can contain event details beyond a minimal 'motion detected' alert.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimisation structure; exact subnode may differ by catalog version.

title: Push-notification metadata discloses occupancy or behavior patterns in transit
description: Even if notification content is minimal, the existence, timing, frequency, and routing metadata of motion alerts can reveal when motion occurs at the home, enabling inference about presence, routines, or unusual activity. This is an implicit disclosure on the data flow itself.
assumptions: Assumes push delivery involves observable metadata to intermediaries or network observers, or that metadata is otherwise exposed beyond strictly necessary parties.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; threat applicability is strong but the precise subnode may vary across LINDDUN Pro versions.

title: Notification content may be exposed on the recipient device to unintended viewers
description: On receipt, the homeowner's phone may display the motion alert on the lock screen, notification shade, wearable, or shared device context, disclosing personal information about home activity to bystanders or other device users. The privacy risk arises at the destination because of how the recipient environment presents or stores the notification.
assumptions: Assumes the phone or connected devices may show notification previews or retain notification history accessible to others.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort; destination-side disclosure via presentation/storage is the intended classification.

title: Repeated motion alerts can be linked to build a behavioral profile
description: A sequence of notifications on this flow can be correlated over time to link events to the same household and derive routines such as wake/sleep times, absences, or occupancy patterns. The threat stems from linkability of multiple alert instances and their metadata.
assumptions: Assumes alerts are attributable to the same account/household through identifiers, routing, or stable metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is approximate; linkability across repeated events clearly applies.

title: Motion-alert notifications can identify the household or resident
description: Notification payload or metadata may contain stable identifiers such as account IDs, device tokens, property names, camera labels, or other contextual details that allow the homeowner, household, or address to be identified by intermediaries or observers.
assumptions: Assumes identifiers or sufficiently specific context are present in payload or associated delivery metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; identifiability depends on implementation details of payload and push infrastructure.

title: Homeowner may be unaware of notification visibility and retention on their device
description: The recipient may not understand that motion alerts can appear on lock screens, sync to wearables, or remain in notification history, reducing transparency about how personal data is exposed after delivery. This creates an unawareness threat at the destination.
assumptions: Assumes the app or service does not clearly explain notification preview, cross-device display, or retention behavior.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; unawareness is plausible but depends on UX and notice design.

title: Backend may send motion notifications without valid or granular user choice
description: If the backend pushes motion-detected alerts without the homeowner's explicit, current, and granular preferences for notification categories, timing, or content detail, the sharing may exceed the user's consent or chosen privacy settings.
assumptions: Assumes notification preferences or consent are relevant for this service and may be absent, stale, or insufficiently granular.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on product design and legal basis; included because notification sending often relies on user-configurable choices.

title: Backend shares analytics that may remain linkable to a user or device across disclosures
description: Even if described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend's act of sending analytics to the vendor can enable linking of records over time or across datasets if stable device, account, cohort, campaign, or pseudonymous identifiers are included, or if aggregation is too granular.
assumptions: Assumes the payload may contain persistent or quasi-persistent identifiers, fine-grained dimensions, or small-cell aggregates that permit correlation.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is based on best judgement; applicability depends on the actual fields and aggregation thresholds used.

title: Analytics payload or flow metadata may identify users, devices, or the app operator in transit
description: Data in transit may reveal identifying information directly in the payload or indirectly through metadata such as endpoint, tenant, API keys, or unique analytics dimensions. Even aggregated analytics can identify a person or device when cohorts are small or dimensions are unique.
assumptions: Assumes transport or intermediary visibility to payload metadata, headers, routing information, or insufficient aggregation/anonymization.
uncertainty_note: If strong transport protection and minimization are in place, this threat is reduced; tree-node id is approximate.

title: Vendor can link received analytics with other customer or third-party datasets
description: At receipt, the cloud analytics vendor may correlate the analytics with its existing telemetry, identifiers, or other datasets, enabling cross-context linkage of user/device behavior beyond the original purpose of collection.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor has access to additional datasets or service-side identifiers and is technically or contractually able to combine them.
uncertainty_note: Applies especially where the vendor operates multi-tenant analytics platforms or enriches customer data.

title: Vendor may infer or determine identities from supposedly aggregated analytics
description: The recipient may be able to single out or identify individuals, households, or devices from small cohorts, rare usage patterns, location/time combinations, or by combining the analytics with auxiliary information.
assumptions: Assumes aggregation is not sufficiently privacy-preserving and that auxiliary data is available to the vendor.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; risk depends strongly on k-anonymity thresholds, dimensionality, and auxiliary data.

title: Received analytics may disclose sensitive behavior or attributes
description: Usage analytics can reveal behavioral patterns, interests, routines, health-related app use, or other sensitive attributes, especially when segmented by device, geography, time, or feature usage. The disclosure occurs when the vendor receives and can inspect these analytics.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics dimensions or metrics are rich enough to expose sensitive traits or behaviors.
uncertainty_note: Whether the disclosed attributes are sensitive depends on the app domain and the granularity of the analytics.

title: Vendor may process analytics for purposes users do not expect
description: Once received, the analytics vendor may use the data for service improvement, benchmarking, model training, fraud detection, or other secondary purposes that are not transparent to users and may exceed their expectations for app analytics.
assumptions: Assumes notices, contracts, or product settings do not clearly constrain downstream purposes.
uncertainty_note: This is a common risk for third-party analytics, but actual applicability depends on contractual and configuration controls.

title: Sharing analytics with the vendor may be incompatible with consent, notice, or data-minimization commitments
description: The destination's receipt and processing of analytics may violate privacy policy statements, consent choices, regional transfer restrictions, or minimization/retention obligations if the vendor receives more data than necessary or for an insufficiently disclosed purpose.
assumptions: Assumes applicable legal or policy constraints exist and that the transfer is not fully covered by a valid legal basis and transparent notice.
uncertainty_note: Compliance conclusions depend on jurisdiction, consent design, contract terms, and the exact analytics fields shared.

title: Linkability via retrieval metadata on the video-fetch flow
description: The retrieval flow can expose metadata such as homeowner/account identifier, device identifier, clip identifier, timestamps, IP address, and access patterns. Observers of the flow or intermediaries could correlate repeated fetches to the same household, camera, or event history, linking separate actions and sessions together.
assumptions: Applies if flow metadata is observable by network intermediaries, logs, analytics, or other components handling the transfer, even if payload content is protected.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the specific Linkability subtree for this interaction.

title: Identifiability of the homeowner through video retrieval traffic
description: The act of retrieving a stored clip may reveal the identity or singled-out status of a homeowner through identifiers in requests, authenticated session data, network metadata, or uniquely identifying clip references. Even without inspecting the full video, the flow may permit identifying which user or household is accessing which footage.
assumptions: Assumes identifiers or distinctive metadata are present in the request/response path or associated logs.
uncertainty_note: Specific Identifiability subtree node was not provided in context; node id is approximate.

title: Backend learns sensitive household behavior from retrieved video
description: When P2 retrieves and processes the stored clip, it may infer private information about occupants, visitors, routines, presence at home, or incidents captured in the footage. This exceeds mere transport and arises from the backend's ability to inspect or derive knowledge from the video content.
assumptions: Applies if the backend can access plaintext video or derived metadata and uses it beyond what is strictly necessary to serve playback.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is approximate because the relevant Detectability/Disclosure subtree was not included in the retrieved snippets.

title: Disclosure of video content or derived metadata at the backend
description: The mobile app backend receives highly sensitive video footage and may disclose it to unauthorized parties through insecure handling, excessive internal access, verbose logging, debugging copies, onward sharing to analytics/support systems, or weak access controls on temporary storage and processing.
assumptions: Applies if P2 stores, caches, logs, or redistributes the clip or extracted metadata during playback handling.
uncertainty_note: Specific Disclosure of information subtree node is best-effort due to missing detailed tree context.

title: Unawareness of backend-side retrieval and processing of stored clips
description: Homeowners may be unaware that, when they request playback, the backend retrieves, may temporarily cache, inspect, log, or otherwise process the clip before delivery. If this processing is not transparent, users may not understand who accesses the footage and for what purposes.
assumptions: Applies where notices, UI explanations, or privacy documentation do not clearly describe backend retrieval, caching, logging, or secondary processing.
uncertainty_note: Specific Unawareness subtree node is approximate; context did not include the detailed U tree.

title: Violation of storage limitation through backend retention of retrieved clips
description: After retrieving the stored video for playback, P2 may retain temporary copies, caches, logs, thumbnails, or derived metadata longer than necessary for the playback purpose. Such retention would violate the storage limitation principle.
assumptions: Applies if backend caching, debugging artifacts, or operational logs persist beyond the minimum necessary period.
